q: A scandal in 1985 emptied export markets of Austrian sweet wine, after bulk lots sold as Spatlese and Auslese were found doctored to counterfeit the weight and sweetness of a Pradikat wine. What had been stirred into them?
exp: Diethylene glycol is syrupy and sweet, so a small dose made thin wine taste like an Auslese, and the routine analyses of the day were not looking for it. Newspapers called it antifreeze, which is properly ethylene glycol and a different compound, while methanol belongs to an Italian case the year afterwards that did kill people. No deaths were traced to the Austrian wines, but exports collapsed within weeks and took the Burgenland sweet wine trade down with them, which is much of why the country rebuilt itself around dry wine.

q: A large, very shallow steppe lake on the Hungarian border fogs the vineyards around it in most autumns. Which Austrian lake?
exp: Water barely a metre or two deep evaporates readily and blankets the flat land around Rust and Illmitz in mist. Botrytis is close to an annual event there, which is unusual anywhere in the world.

q: Between Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, Austria's ladder holds a rung that Germany's does not. What is it called?
exp: Ausbruch is the speciality of Rust on the Neusiedlersee, traditionally made by pouring fresh must or wine over botrytised berries to draw their sugar out. Smaragd is a Wachau ripeness term rather than a legal Pradikat.

q: Reed mats or straw hold the bunches for at least three months of drying under an Austrian Pradikat of its own. Which one?
exp: Strohwein and its synonym Schilfwein cover the same practice, reed being the local alternative to straw around the Neusiedlersee. Bergwein is not a ripeness level at all but a designation for fruit off steep slopes.

q: Frozen grapes go into the press solid and only a trickle of syrup runs out. What is left behind in the press?
opts: Frozen alcohol, which would otherwise dilute the wine
Ice crystals of water, holding back most of the volume
Crystals of frozen sugar, which are discarded
Frozen acid, leaving a softer juice
exp: Water freezes at a higher temperature than a sugar solution, so the pure water in the berry turns to ice while the sugary syrup stays liquid. Pressing long and hard against that block is the whole trick, and the syrup that runs out can be a fifth of what the same fruit would have given unfrozen.

q: Eiswein grapes in Germany must go into the press still frozen. Which temperature is the accepted threshold for picking?
exp: German law asks only that the fruit be frozen at harvest and at pressing; minus seven is the working threshold, cold enough to hold back most of the water as ice and lift the must to Beerenauslese weight. Canada writes its own figure into the VQA rules, one degree lower still at minus eight.

q: Freshly picked healthy grapes are put in a freezer overnight and pressed the next morning. Why can the result not be sold as Eiswein?
opts: The temperature reached was too low for the style
Eiswein may only be made from Riesling grapes
The freeze has to happen naturally, out on the vine
exp: Artificial freezing is called cryoextraction and is legal in some regions as a way of rescuing a rain-diluted harvest, but it forfeits the name. The risk that the freeze never comes is the point of the wine.

q: Grapes hang unpicked into December while the grower waits for a hard frost. What can go wrong in the meantime?
opts: The berries pass their sugar back into the vine
The vine itself is usually killed by the hard frost
Birds, wind and rot can take the crop first
The acidity falls away to nothing while the fruit hangs
exp: Nets go over the rows and the wait can run past New Year, and every week that passes takes a little more of the crop. A mild winter means no harvest at all, which is why the wines cost what they do and why some years simply produce none.

q: Set beside a botrytised wine of the same sweetness, an ice wine tastes strikingly different. What marks it out?
opts: Much lower acidity and a heavier, more viscous texture
A distinctly oxidative, nutty character, as in an old sherry
Noticeable tannin from extended skin contact
Pure primary fruit and searing acidity, none of it from rot
exp: Nothing has grown on the fruit, so the wine tastes of the grape it came from: green apple, pear and citrus from Riesling, tropical fruit from Vidal. None of the honeyed, marmalade or savoury notes of rot are there. Concentration without transformation is the whole idea.

q: A thick-skinned French-American hybrid holds onto its bunches through a Canadian winter better than any vinifera. Which variety?
exp: Vidal's tough skin resists splitting and its bunches stay attached long after Riesling would have dropped its fruit. It gives the mango and pineapple style most Canadian icewine drinkers know.

q: Bunches are laid out in an airy loft for three or four months after harvest and lose a third of their weight. What is that Italian practice called?
exp: The dried fruit is pressed in the depths of winter, giving a must so concentrated that fermentation is slow and stubborn. Governo and ripasso both add something back to a finished wine, and saignee bleeds juice off red skins.

q: A sweet red from the hills north of Verona comes from grapes dried until midwinter, with the fermentation halted while sugar remains. Which wine?
exp: Recioto is the older of the two great dried-grape wines of the zone, and Amarone began as a barrel of it that was allowed to ferment right out. Amaro means bitter, which is how the dry version struck those who first tasted it.

q: Dried Garganega makes a sweet golden white in the hills east of Verona. Which wine is it?
exp: Same grape and same hills as dry Soave, with the bunches dried right through the winter first. Torcolato is Breganze's dried-grape sweet white from Vespaiola, and Sciacchetra comes from the Cinque Terre.

q: Bunches hang from rafters through the winter, and the wine then spends years in small sealed barrels left deliberately part-empty. Which Tuscan speciality?
exp: The barrels, called caratelli, are sealed and stored in a loft, so the wine swings through summer heat and winter cold for three years or more. That cycling gives the nutty, caramel, dried-fig character.

q: Each caratello for Vin Santo is charged with a residue held back from the previous batch. What is that starter called?
exp: The madre is a sludge of yeast and lees carried from barrel to barrel across generations, and it is what gets a fermentation moving in a must too sweet for ordinary yeast. Every cellar's madre is its own.

q: On a windy volcanic island between Sicily and Tunisia, Zibibbo grapes are dried in the sun for a deep amber sweet wine. Which grape is Zibibbo?
exp: Pantelleria trains its vines in hollows scooped out of the ground to shelter them from the wind, and the fruit is dried on open racks. Muscat of Alexandria is the coarser of the two great Muscats, but on this island it is magnificent.
